entry: Anthology of twenty-four stories in [[Middle English]] by [[Geoffrey Chaucer]]. The stories are mostly in verse and are presented as a storytelling contest among pilgrims traveling from London to Canterbury to visit the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral. They were written between 1387 and 1400. Chaucer planned about 120 stories, four from each pilgrim, but most scholars think the work was left incomplete. The Tales are regarded as Chaucer's magnum opus and one of the paramount works of [[English literature]]. They may have helped establish the English vernacular in mainstream literature, as opposed to French or [[Latin]]. The work survives in 84 manuscripts and four incunabula. William Caxton's 1476 printed edition was one of the first books printed in England; only 10 copies are known to exist.

1957 children's book by [[Dr. Seuss]]. A tall anthropomorphic cat entertains two children on a rainy day while their mother is away. Theodor Geisel wrote it in response to debate over traditional primers, after William Spaulding of Houghton Mifflin asked him for a more entertaining primer. Random House published the trade edition, and the book sold over a million copies within three years. Its success led to the creation of Beginner Books. It was adapted into a 1971 animated television special and a 2003 live-action film.

1951 American coming-of-age novel by [[J. D. Salinger]]. Holden Caulfield, an expelled prep school student, narrates several days of wandering around New York City. The novel was partly published in serial form in 1945–1946 before appearing in full in 1951. Originally intended for adults, it is often read by adolescents for its themes of angst, alienation and superficiality in society. Holden has become an icon of teenage rebellion. About one million copies are sold each year, with total sales of more than 65 million. [[Time (magazine)|Time]]'s 2005 list of the 100 best English-language novels written since 1923 included it, and Modern Library named it one of the 100 best English-language novels of the 20th century. In 2003 it ranked 15th in the [[BBC]]'s survey "The Big Read."

American [[Country music|country music]] band from [[Dallas]], Texas, formerly the Dixie Chicks. Sisters Martie Maguire and Emily Strayer founded the group in 1989, and Natalie Maines joined as lead singer in 1995. In 2003, while on stage in London, the band criticized President [[George W. Bush]] and the imminent [[Iraq War]], provoking a backlash. The group reunited in 2016 and removed "Dixie" from its name in 2020. They have received 13 [[Grammy Awards]] and charted 22 times on the Billboard Hot Country Songs charts. They are the best-selling all-woman band, with 33 million certified albums sold by July 2020.

Series of seven portal fantasy novels by [[C. S. Lewis]], published between October 1950 and September 1956. The books are set in Narnia, a world of magic, mythical beasts and talking animals. Children from the real world are transported there, and the lion Aslan often calls on them to protect Narnia from evil. The books span Narnia's history, from its creation in *The Magician's Nephew* to its destruction in *The Last Battle*. *The Last Battle* earned Lewis the 1956 Carnegie Medal. Lewis drew on [[Myth|mythology]], medieval literature and [[Cosmology|cosmology]], and preferred the term "supposition" to "allegory." Critics cite perceived inconsistencies, gender stereotyping and racial representation, while defenders argue that female characters are often portrayed heroically. The series, Lewis's best-selling work, has sold approximately 120 million copies and has been adapted for radio, television, film and video games.

headword: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
sort_key: church of jesus christ of latter day saints
entry: Largest denomination of the Latter Day Saint movement, founded by [[Joseph Smith]] in 1830. Headquartered in [[Salt Lake City]], Utah, it reports more than 17.5 million members as of 2024. Its theology is restorationist and nontrinitarian, and its scriptures include the [[Bible]] and the Book of Mormon. After Smith's death in 1844, most followers sided with [[Brigham Young]], who led the church to its current headquarters. The church's practice of [[Polygamy|polygamy]] was curtailed in 1890 and officially rescinded in 1904. Members are known as Latter-day Saints, and women are not ordained to the priesthood.

English [[Punk rock|punk rock]] band formed in London in 1976. Billed as "The Only Band That Matters," the group fused punk with [[Reggae|reggae]], dub, funk, ska and rockabilly, and is considered one of the most influential acts of the original British punk wave. Their album *London Calling* (1979) was named the best album of the 1980s by [[Rolling Stone]]. *Combat Rock* (1982) included the US top-10 hit "Rock the Casbah." The band was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2003.

American multinational beverage corporation headquartered in [[Atlanta]], Georgia. The original drink was developed in 1886 by pharmacist John Stith Pemberton and contained [[Caffeine|caffeine]] and [[Cocaine|cocaine]]. Asa Griggs Candler bought the [[Coca-Cola]] formula and brand and incorporated the company in Atlanta in 1892. The company mainly sells syrup concentrate to bottlers with exclusive territories. It is listed on the [[New York Stock Exchange]]. The company has drawn criticism over sustainability and the health effects of its products. A 2024 study found that over 11% of branded plastic pollution came from Coca-Cola.

Political pamphlet by [[Karl Marx]] and [[Friedrich Engels]], first published in 1848. It was commissioned by the Communist League and published in London, amid the [[Revolutions of 1848]] in Europe. It states that "the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles," and argues that [[Capitalism|capitalism]] is marked by the exploitation of the proletariat by the ruling [[Bourgeoisie|bourgeoisie]]. It predicts that a revolution will bring [[Communism|communism]], a classless society in which "the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all." The work combines philosophical [[Materialism|materialism]] with the Hegelian [[Dialectic|dialectical method]] to analyze European society through successive modes of production. Its closing line, "Workers of the world, unite!," became a famous slogan of working-class solidarity, and the pamphlet has become one of the world's most influential political documents.

Adventure novel by [[Alexandre Dumas]], serialized from 1844 to 1846. Edmond Dantès, a young sailor falsely accused of treason, escapes from the Château d'If, recovers a hidden treasure and transforms himself into a wealthy nobleman. Under the name Count of Monte Cristo, he pursues [[Revenge|revenge]] against those who betrayed him, then abandons it in favor of redemption. The story spans 1815–1839, from the [[Hundred Days]] to the reign of [[Louis Philippe I]]. Its themes include hope, justice, vengeance, mercy and forgiveness. Its serialization drew large audiences, and it has been adapted into many films and television series.

Fresco by [[Michelangelo]] on the ceiling of the [[Sistine Chapel]]. It illustrates the creation narrative from the [[Book of Genesis]], in which God gives life to [[Adam]], the first man. It is chronologically the fourth in the series of Genesis panels painted for [[Pope Julius II]] in 1508–1512. The ceiling composition contains over 300 figures and forms part of a larger scheme representing the doctrine of the [[Catholic Church]]. It is one of the most replicated religious paintings of all time.

1953 play by [[Arthur Miller]]. It is a partly fictionalized account of the [[Salem witch trials]] in the Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1692 to 1693. Miller wrote it as an allegory for [[McCarthyism]], when the United States government persecuted people accused of being communists. Miller was questioned by the House Committee on Un-American Activities in 1956 and convicted of contempt of Congress. It opened on Broadway at the Martin Beck Theatre on January 22, 1953, and won the Tony Award for Best Play. It is regarded as a central work in the canon of American drama.

English rock band formed in Crawley in 1976 by Robert Smith and Lol Tolhurst. Smith has been the band's only constant member, and its 1979 debut, *Three Imaginary Boys*, placed it at the forefront of British post-punk. The band achieved mainstream success with *Disintegration* (1989) and *Wish* (1992). *Pornography* (1982) had a strong influence on gothic rock. The band has released 14 studio albums and sold more than 30 million records. It was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2019. *Songs of a Lost World* (2024) topped charts in multiple countries.

2008 superhero film directed by [[Christopher Nolan]]. It is the sequel to *Batman Begins* (2005) and stars [[Christian Bale]] as [[Batman]]. Batman, police lieutenant Jim Gordon and district attorney Harvey Dent try to dismantle [[Organized crime|organized crime]] in Gotham City, but the Joker derails their efforts. [[Heath Ledger|Ledger]]'s performance as the Joker won posthumous Academy, BAFTA and Golden Globe awards. It was the first comic-book film to receive major acting awards, and it was the first major motion picture filmed with high-resolution IMAX cameras. The [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry in 2020.

headword: The Dark Side of the Moon
entry: Eighth studio album by [[Pink Floyd]], released in 1973. Bassist [[Roger Waters]] conceived it around the pressures of the band's arduous lifestyle and the mental health problems of former member Syd Barrett. It was recorded in London in 1972 and 1973. The album explores conflict, greed, time, death and mental illness. Its sleeve, designed by Storm Thorgerson, depicts a [[Prism (optics)|prismatic]] spectrum. By 2013 it had sold over 45 million copies worldwide, the best-selling album of the 1970s. The [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the United States National Recording Registry in 2012.

1978 war drama film directed by Michael Cimino. It follows three Russian-American steelworkers from Clairton, Pennsylvania, whose lives are upended by the [[Vietnam War]]. Its cast includes [[Robert De Niro]], [[Christopher Walken]], John Savage and [[Meryl Streep]]. The film won five of its nine nominations at the [[Academy Awards]], including Best Picture and Best Director. It cost $15 million, going over budget and schedule, and grossed $49 million. It was selected by the [[Library of Congress]] for the National Film Registry in 1996.

American rock band formed in [[Los Angeles]] in 1965. It took its name from [[Aldous Huxley]]'s book *The Doors of Perception*, itself a reference to a quote by [[William Blake]]. Vocalist [[Jim Morrison]] and the band recorded six studio albums in five years, including *The Doors* (1967) and *L.A. Woman* (1971). Morrison died in 1971 in uncertain circumstances, and the band continued as a trio, releasing two more albums until disbanding in 1973. The band was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1993 and has sold over 100 million records worldwide.

Series of action role-playing [[Video game|video games]] developed mainly by Bethesda Game Studios. Each game takes place on the continent of Tamriel, a setting that blends a Roman-like empire with [[Magic (supernatural)|magic]] and mythological creatures. The games focus on free-form gameplay in an open world. Beginning with *The Elder Scrolls: Arena* in 1994, the series has sold more than 90 million copies. *Morrowind* (2002), *Oblivion* (2006) and [[The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim|Skyrim]] (2011) each won Game of the Year awards. The 2014 massively multiplayer online game *The Elder Scrolls Online* extends the series.

2011 action role-playing video game, the fifth main installment of [[The Elder Scrolls]]. Set in the northern province of Skyrim, it follows the Last Dragonborn in a quest to defeat Alduin, a prophesied world-destroying dragon. Its open world, based on [[Scandinavia]], lets players ignore or postpone the main storyline indefinitely. It was released for [[Microsoft Windows]], PlayStation 3 and [[Xbox 360]] on November 11, 2011. It earned critical acclaim on release. It is considered one of the greatest video games ever made, and total sales have reached 65 million copies.

State of emergency in [[India]], 1975–1977. Prime Minister [[Indira Gandhi]] proposed it, and President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed issued it under Article 352 of the [[Constitution of India]] on grounds of an "internal disturbance." It let the prime minister rule by decree, cancel elections and suspend [[Civil liberties|civil liberties]]. The [[Censorship|press was censored]], and more than 100,000 political opponents, journalists and dissenters were imprisoned. A mass campaign for vasectomy was led by her son Sanjay Gandhi. It lasted from June 25, 1975, to March 21, 1977.

1980 epic space opera film directed by Irvin Kershner. It is the second film in the [[Star Wars]] series, in which the Rebel Alliance battles the Galactic Empire. Luke Skywalker trains to master the Force, and the climax, in which [[Darth Vader]] reveals he is Luke's father, is often ranked among cinema's greatest plot twists. Released on May 21, 1980, it was the year's highest-grossing film, with a worldwide gross of $549–$550 million. It is now often regarded as the best film in the series.

1973 supernatural horror film directed by [[William Friedkin]]. William Peter Blatty adapted his 1971 novel for the film, which follows the demonic possession of a young girl and an exorcism by two Catholic priests. Its troubled production, marked by injuries and mishaps, led to a belief that it was cursed. It was the first horror film nominated for Best Picture at the [[Academy Awards]], and Blatty won Best Adapted Screenplay. The [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry in 2010.

American animated sitcom by [[Hanna-Barbera]]. Set in the [[Stone Age]] town of Bedrock, it follows the Flintstone and Rubble families. Its humor comes largely from anachronism, placing a modern suburban society in prehistory. It premiered on ABC on September 30, 1960, as the first animated series with a prime-time slot on television. Its producers had earned seven [[Academy Awards]] for *Tom and Jerry*. It was the most financially successful and longest-running network animated series for three decades.

Set of four violin concertos by [[Antonio Vivaldi]], each evoking a season of the year. Composed around 1718–1723, when Vivaldi was court chapel master in Mantua, they were published in 1725 in [[Amsterdam]] as part of *Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione*. Vivaldi depicted flowing creeks, singing birds, buzzing flies, storms and frozen landscapes, a revolution in musical conception. He published the concertos with [[Sonnet|sonnets]], possibly written by Vivaldi himself, that describe each season. The concertos are among the earliest and most detailed examples of program music. Each concerto has three movements, fast–slow–fast, and each sonnet has three matching sections. A performance of all four takes about 40–43 minutes. The first proper electrical recording was made in 1942 by Bernardino Molinari. It is the best known of Vivaldi's works.

American television [[Sitcom|sitcom]] that aired on [[NBC]] from 1990 to 1996. [[Will Smith]] stars as a fictionalized version of himself, a street-smart teenager from West Philadelphia who is sent to live with his wealthy uncle and aunt in Bel-Air. It contrasts his [[Working class|working-class]] background with the [[Upper class|upper-class]] world of the Banks family. The series ran for 148 episodes over six seasons and was a major commercial success for NBC. Smith and James Avery were the only actors to appear in every episode. Its premise came from the life of music manager Benny Medina, who pitched it to [[Quincy Jones]].
